title: How to Practise for the 11+
description: Short daily sessions, words met in reading, and mistakes revisited: a practical routine for 11+ vocabulary that fits around family life.
standfirst: Effective practice is not longer practice. It is the same small loop — meet a word, try it, meet it again — repeated often enough that it sticks.

sections.heading: Little and often beats long and occasional
paragraphs: Memory consolidates between sessions, not during them, so five focused minutes a day outperform an hour on Sunday. Pick a slot that already exists — after breakfast, before dinner — and protect it the way you would any other appointment.

End every session while it is still going well, even mid-list. Stopping on a success is what makes a child willing to start tomorrow, and willingness to start tomorrow is the whole game across a year.

sections.heading: Meet words in the wild, not just on lists
paragraphs: A word on a list is recognised; a word met in a story is remembered. When you practise a word, follow it into a sentence: use it at dinner, spot it in a book, notice it on a sign. Each meeting in a new context strengthens the memory more than another look at the same card.

Reading remains the best vocabulary teacher available. A child who reads for pleasure meets more new words in a month than any list contains, and meets each of them doing a job in a sentence — which is how the papers test them.

sections.heading: Make mistakes the plan, not the accident
paragraphs: A wrong answer is the most useful moment in a session: it shows exactly which word is not known yet. Treat it that way out loud. Say what the right answer means, use it in a sentence together, and let the word come back in a few days rather than drilling it on the spot.

Keep a visible record of words that slipped — a sheet on the fridge, a list to print. Watching that list shrink is concrete proof of progress, and proof is what keeps a nine-year-old going through the slow middle months.

sections.heading: Say words aloud
paragraphs: Hearing a word, saying it, and seeing it are three different memories of the same thing, and three memories beat one. Ask your child to pronounce new words and use each in a sentence of their own. A sentence of their own is the test that matters: a child who can use a word knows it, however they scored on options.

If a pronunciation is uncertain, look it up together rather than guessing past it. Mispronounced words are harder to recognise in a listening task and easier to avoid in writing, which quietly shrinks the vocabulary you worked to build.

sections.heading: Keep it kind
paragraphs: Praise the showing up, not the score. Streaks break, hard weeks happen, and a child who believes effort counts will practise through both. Never use a missed word as evidence in an argument, and never compare siblings' scores — comparison teaches children to hide mistakes, and hidden mistakes cannot be revised.
If practice regularly ends badly, change the practice: shorter sessions, easier words, a different time of day. The routine serves the child, never the reverse.
